mcqs.question: A team has Circle/Square shapes and Vector/Raster renderers, and both dimensions are expected to grow. Why does Bridge avoid the subclass explosion that plain inheritance would cause here?
options: It generates renderer code automatically at compile time
It puts shape and renderer logic into two independent hierarchies connected by composition, so a new shape or new renderer needs exactly one new class, not one per combination
It only allows one renderer to exist at a time
It merges Shape and Renderer into a single class
mcqs.explanation: Bridge's core mechanism is splitting the two varying dimensions into separate hierarchies joined by a has-a relationship, so growth in either dimension is additive, not multiplicative. There's no code generation, no single-renderer restriction, and merging the hierarchies is exactly what Bridge avoids.

mcqs.question: In the Flyweight pattern, what distinguishes intrinsic state from extrinsic state?
options: Intrinsic state is stored in a database; extrinsic state is stored in memory
Intrinsic state is always numeric; extrinsic state is always a string
There is no real distinction — both terms describe the same thing
Intrinsic state is shared and immutable across instances; extrinsic state is unique per occurrence and supplied from outside the shared object
mcqs.explanation: This is the exact definition Flyweight relies on: intrinsic state (like a glyph's shape at a given font/size) is shared and safe to reuse; extrinsic state (like its position on a page) varies per use and must be supplied by the caller, not stored on the shared object. The other options aren't how the pattern defines these terms.

mcqs.question: Why does GlyphFactory.get() check a pool keyed by (char, font, size) before creating a new Glyph?
options: To guarantee every character in the document gets a unique object
To make the document render in alphabetical order
To avoid allocating a new object for every occurrence of the same char/font/size combination, reusing one shared instance instead
To enforce that only lowercase letters can be rendered
mcqs.explanation: The pool is exactly Flyweight's memory-saving mechanism — reuse one shared instance for every occurrence of an identical intrinsic-state combination instead of allocating a new object each time. It doesn't guarantee uniqueness (the opposite, actually), doesn't restrict character case, and has nothing to do with render order.

mcqs.question: A team designing a new cross-platform rendering library from scratch wants shapes and renderers to evolve independently from day one. A different team is stuck bolting a modern interface onto a vendor SDK they can't modify. Which pattern fits each, respectively?
options: Both teams should use Adapter
Both teams should use Bridge
Bridge for the first team (designed upfront, both sides controlled); Adapter for the second (retrofitted onto an existing, uncontrolled interface)
Adapter for the first team; Bridge for the second
mcqs.explanation: Bridge is chosen upfront when you control and are designing both sides to vary independently; Adapter is chosen after the fact when you're stuck matching an interface you don't control. Swapping them, or using just one pattern for both scenarios, misses the timing/control distinction that actually separates them.

mcqs.question: A shared Glyph flyweight gets a mutable color field so callers can 'just update it' per use. What bug does this introduce?
options: Changing the color for one occurrence of a shared glyph silently changes it for every other occurrence sharing that same pooled instance
The glyph pool grows unbounded in size
The GlyphFactory stops caching new glyphs
Rendering becomes slower but otherwise correct
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic Flyweight cross-talk bug: mutating shared (intrinsic) state affects every user of that shared instance at once, since they're literally the same object in memory. It doesn't change pool size or caching behavior, and it's a correctness bug, not just a performance one.
